toc.title: Habit three: journaling about painful things without the capacity for it
Habit five: just feeling your feelings
What these five have in common

blocks.p: The self-help industry sells doing as the cure: more habits, more discipline, more effort. And that makes sense. Change doesn't happen unless you do something different. So it comes down to what that different thing is, and whether it will lead to the change you want.

Let's explore five common self-help habits you might already be doing that maybe aren't helping, or are making things worse without you realizing it. For a nervous system that's already overwhelmed, already in sympathetic flight or fight, freeze overdrive, or shutdown collapse, more doing is not necessarily helpful. More doing might mean more overwhelm, more frustration, and more defeat.

This is not an attack on these self-help practices universally. Some of them are great for people who already have the capacity. It's those who are stuck in a defensive state that I'm more concerned about here.

The first habit is forced positive affirmations, or toxic positivity. This can look like standing in front of the mirror repeating "I am worthy. I am safe. I am enough" while your body is screaming the opposite. It can look like trying to replace every negative thought with a positive one. It can look like gratitude journaling as an emotional override, or conjuring positivity from the universe through your thinking.

"Positive thinking, Justin? What could be the issue with positive thinking?" Well, the first thing that comes to mind is that it's not real. Just thinking something positive, even repeatedly, does not make it so. Trying to replace negative thoughts with positive ones sounds absolutely exhausting, and frustrating beyond belief. And no, you can't summon positivity through universal conjuration. That's called wishing.

Is it okay to wish for things? Yes, sure. Go right ahead, especially if it's your birthday. If you have a wish, if you have a want, go ahead. Journal about your gratitude, if you have gratitude to journal about. Think positively when you have positive thoughts. Tell yourself something nice when you see yourself in the mirror, if you have something nice to say. In other words, when it's real, yes, do those things.

Otherwise, when your body is in a defensive state like flight, fight, shutdown, or freeze, you probably lack positivity, nice things to say to yourself, and gratitude. This is true when you're triggered into one of these defensive states, but I'm more focused on your baseline defensive state.

When you tell yourself the opposite, saying something positive when you don't really feel that way, it creates a mismatch between your thoughts and your nervous system state. Your brain says, "I'm fine, and everything's going to be okay," but your body doesn't believe it. In essence, you're lying to yourself. You cannot trick your body into safety by changing the words in your brain.

This mismatch is not neutral. I'd say it's disrespectful. You're essentially telling your body to shut up. That's not safety; that's invalidation. And invalidation only adds friction to the process, making things worse. I'd bet you have received, or are receiving, this type of invalidation from somebody else in your life, so the sooner you can stop doing it to yourself, the better.

Instead of forcing positivity, practice honest acknowledgment: "My body feels tense right now. That makes sense, given what I've been through." That's not negativity. That's accuracy. And accuracy is what builds trust between you and your nervous system.
I hear from so many clients and students that simply acknowledging and normalizing their experiences helps reduce the intensity of those experiences.

The second potentially unhelpful habit is controlled breathwork. I feel like I need to tread carefully with this one, because people love their controlled breathing methods. What's your breath control of choice? Wim Hof? Intense pranayama? Holotropic breathwork? Box breathing with long holds? Something else? There are so many, and they all carry so many promises.

So what's the problem with this, Justin? Controlled breathing suffers from the same essential problem as forced positive thinking: it rejects your body's natural state. If we were to give the two of them personalities, your conscious mind is telling your body, "I know better than you do. You're breathing wrong."

Think about this for a moment, and I think you'll see just how silly it is. Do you, in your conscious thinking mind right now, know how much oxygen you need? Or do your unconscious, autonomic, biological processes know better than your thinking brain? I think the answer is obvious.

Your body is in a dominant defensive state: flight, fight, shutdown, or freeze. And your body breathes based on that state's current needs. Logically, we assume that if we change our breathing, we change our state. And yes, kind of. But the dominant defensive state comes right back, doesn't it?

In a given moment, extending your exhale might help you settle a bit more into stillness and calm. Breathing bigger into your chest might help you increase your mobilization. But your body may not need either of these. And again, you're adding friction to the process. You're rejecting the natural state of your body and what it needs now.

I've begun guiding my clients and students to just notice their natural breath. And once they do that, you know what happens? It changes by itself, in a fairly predictable way. People with higher levels of sympathetic flight or fight, who breathe tightly into their chest, eventually notice their breath going more and more into their belly, naturally. And people in shutdown, who breathe shallowly into their belly, eventually notice more expansion into their chest.
But they don't plan it. These changes happen on their own once we pay attention and stay connected to the present moment.

blocks.h: Habit three: journaling about painful things without the capacity for it

blocks.p: The third habit is journaling about trauma or painful emotions without the capacity for it. People sit down and write detailed accounts of their worst experiences, or meditate on them. "Get it all out on paper," they say. Prompted journals ask: What's your earliest painful memory? Write a letter to your former self right after the traumatic incident. Write a letter to your abuser.

This looks like deep exploratory work, and maybe some people are ready for it, but there's a good chance they're not. And since it looks like deep exploratory work, you might be pushing yourself to do it.
This is memory excavation without a regulated baseline. You're asking yourself to jump into the pool without knowing how to swim or where the ladder is to climb out.

Writing about traumatic details activates the same neural networks as experiencing them. The body doesn't really distinguish between remembering and reliving. If you don't have the ventral vagal capacity to stay anchored in the present moment, you're not processing. You're potentially retraumatizing yourself.

Journaling about painful memories and emotions mirrors the same problem as approaches like EMDR or trauma-focused CBT when they're applied without sufficient emotional regulation skills. The method isn't inherently bad. It's the sequence that's the problem. We need present-moment grounding first. Ideally, we also need more capacity before going into painful experiences.
There are a couple of super easy alternatives if you'd like to start journaling, or change your current journaling practice.
Try journaling on the present moment. What do you hear? What do you see? How is your body breathing? What thoughts pass through your mind? Is there an emotion within you right now?

You can also write about difficult things, but keep it contained. Write less, with less detail. As you build capacity and want to go into details, go ahead, but listen to what your body can handle currently. As you write about the past, make sure you stay anchored to the present. Write a little. When you notice activation rising, pause or stop, and recover. Then, when you're ready, continue, but pause or stop whenever you need to.

This could be a great way to build capacity over time. Over time, you'll need to pause less, as you successfully recover and reregulate when you need to. Pausing and recovering after writing a few words is way more beneficial than forcing your way through five pages of past traumatic agony and feeling it all over again in the present.

The fourth potentially unhelpful habit is rigid morning routines. Listen, there's nothing wrong with routines and structure. That might be exactly what you need. I have my own little routines and structures that I like to follow. Nothing's wrong with that.

However, I want you to ask yourself what your motivation is for your morning routine. Are you suppressing emotion through controlled routines? That's okay for coping, but not helpful for actually making change, which is kind of the entire point of self-help.

Do you really need your 6:00 a.m. smoothie, or is that just something to focus on instead of what really needs your attention, like stress and overwhelm? Do you really need to gratitude journal at 6:15, or is it okay to look out the window silently and admit to yourself that life kind of sucks right now? Are you taking a cold shower for the potential health benefits, or to shock your emotions temporarily out of your system? Are you doing all of this and more because it feels right, or because someone popular online does the same thing?

For a regulated nervous system, or one with mild dysregulation, these routines can be grounding. That's fine. But for a dysregulated one, these routines are at best a coping skill, I'd argue, and potentially yet another demand on a system that simply cannot take any more. It's another thing to get excited about and then fail at, or feel like you're failing at. Another performative thing that looks like actual wellness, but just isn't.

And then what happens when you don't measure up? When you miss a day of the morning routine, or blend the wrong stuff into your morning smoothie? A shame spiral kicks in, and now the thing that was supposed to help you is generating the exact sympathetic arousal and dorsal collapse it was probably supposed to prevent in the first place.

These emotions, like shame and regret and pressure, aren't new. They're already within you, masked by the morning routine. When you miss it, the emotions that have been waiting around, suppressed, come to the surface.

Again, there's nothing wrong with a morning routine, or any routine, and overall I think they're a good idea. Yes, leave the house on time to get to work and to get the kids to school. Yes, wake up at a certain time so you have enough time to get ready for the day. Yes, have breakfast every morning. Basic stuff, and a routine helps with that.

But within that routine, check in with your body and what it actually needs. You might want to start the day super productive, but if you're sluggish, it's not going to happen. Maybe you need silent time and dim lights to wake up. You might want to start the day nice and slow and calm, but if you wake up with stress, that's not going to happen. Maybe you need movement first thing in the morning instead.

You have to listen to your body. Be open to your morning, and to how it needs to change. You might need slow and steady for a few weeks, and then it changes to more active and energized. You don't decide that. Your body's state does. This can change over time as your nervous system becomes less stuck and has more capacity for movement, connection, or slow mindfulness. It can also change with the seasons and daylight saving time.
So instead of being fixed and rigid, allow some spontaneity within your basic morning routine.

blocks.h: Habit five: just feeling your feelings

blocks.p: The last self-help habit I can think of that may be making things worse for you is just feeling your feelings. Yes, I also want you to feel your feelings, but only when you're sufficiently connected to the present moment and ready to. If not, you risk opening the floodgates and drowning.

Feeling your feelings assumes you have the ventral vagal capacity to stay present while also experiencing your emotions. In other words, it assumes your window of tolerance can handle it, and maybe it just can't yet. So you end up in the same spot as when you began.

The alternative is to practice very simple emotional balancing. Touch the edge of the feeling, and then come back to safety in the present moment. Back and forth, like dipping your toe in the water instead of diving into the deep end.

So instead of feeling your feelings as sensation in the body, maybe start with acknowledging your feelings as factual things that exist, without denying them. Instead of diving into the deep end of depression and spending time submerged in heaviness and emptiness and loneliness and numbness, just acknowledge truthfully: "I feel depressed." Then shift your focus back to the present moment, like the sounds around you and the view out your window.

If you can acknowledge it, then you can start going deeper into the water by identifying how it shows up in your body, first generally and then more specifically, and then as sensations. All the while, balance with safety. The ability to feel your feelings, to sit with them, is built progressively through consistent short practices. I don't think it's built through one cathartic explosion or release.

blocks.h: What these five have in common

blocks.p: So what do these all have in common? Each of them asks you to go beyond what you may be capable of.

My recommendation, no matter what you're doing to work on yourself, whether it's these five, going to therapy, working with a coach, or talking with a pastor, is that you work within your capacity, and don't push things too far or too fast.

And remember, self-help gurus are teaching you from their own capacity. They have the capacity to think positively. Good for them, although I don't typically believe it, personally. They love to control their breathing, and they get something out of it. Whatever. They have it within them to journal about their pain. That's fine. They stick to their strict morning routine for whatever reason, and that's cool. They feel their feelings through prolonged meditations. Outstanding. I'm so happy for them.
I don't care whether you do these things or not. It's up to you. I'm mostly concerned with you working within your capacity.

The other thing these have in common is that they treat your thinking brain as the expert on what your body needs. Your thinking brain supposedly knows best about your breath, or your morning routine, or whatever, when really your body might be saying, "Actually, we need something else."

This has been coming up a lot recently in the self-regulation cohorts I lead. I guide students through lessons and practices designed to gradually help them connect with safety and relieve defense. But in a cohort, things are very templated and structured. So I implore students to listen to their capacity during our self-regulation practices. Even though I'm leading, they need to pause when their system tells them it's time to pause. Not just during live practices, but also during homework, when they listen to prerecorded meditations that are also designed to widen their capacity.

blocks.p: If you're recognizing yourself in any of these five habits, that's not a reason to feel shame, especially if you like doing them. And if you can acknowledge that they're unhelpful, that's also not a reason to feel shame. That's just awareness. And awareness is the first step toward doing something different.
